canonical_statement: The trial evaluated whether adding valsartan to prescribed standard therapy for chronic heart failure would reduce long-term morbidity and mortality.
Val-HeFT was a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group trial conducted at 302 centers in 16 countries.
An independent end-points committee adjudicated all primary end points, and an independent data and safety monitoring board reviewed biannual interim analyses.

Eligible participants were adults at least 18 years old with heart failure for at least three months, NYHA class II-IV symptoms, clinical stability, and at least two weeks on a fixed-dose heart-failure regimen.

canonical_statement: Eligibility required left ventricular ejection fraction below 40% and left ventricular end-diastolic internal dimension greater than 2.9 cm/m² of body-surface area.

canonical_statement: Before randomization, patients completed a 2- to 4-week single-blind placebo run-in to confirm eligibility, clinical stability, and compliance.
Valsartan was started at 40 mg orally twice daily and doubled every two weeks to a target of 160 mg twice daily when tolerated.

exposures.details: Target dose; initiated at 40 mg twice daily and doubled every two weeks as tolerated.

canonical_statement: The comparator was matching oral placebo with dose adjustments performed in parallel with valsartan.

exposures.details: Dose adjusted in parallel with valsartan.

canonical_statement: Randomization was stratified by baseline beta-blocker use to balance beta-blocker therapy between treatment groups.
Dose escalation required standing systolic blood pressure at least 90 mm Hg, no hypotensive symptoms, and serum creatinine below 2.0 mg/dL or no more than 50% above baseline.
Follow-up visits occurred at 2, 4, and 6 months and every 3 months thereafter.
One primary end point was all-cause mortality.

The co-primary mortality-morbidity composite was death, resuscitated cardiac arrest, hospitalization for heart failure, or at least four hours of intravenous inotropic or vasodilator therapy without hospitalization.

outcome.definition: Death from any cause, cardiac arrest with resuscitation, hospitalization for heart failure, or intravenous inotropic/vasodilator therapy for at least 4 hours without hospitalization

canonical_statement: Secondary cardiovascular outcomes included changes in ejection fraction, NYHA class, quality of life, and signs and symptoms of heart failure.

The two primary end points were analyzed with multiplicity adjustment; mortality also used O’Brien-Fleming alpha spending for five biannual interim analyses, with a final two-sided significance level of 0.02.

Primary end points were compared by log-rank tests, and Cox regression estimated treatment effects with prespecified baseline covariates including NYHA class, ejection fraction, heart-failure cause, age, ACE-inhibitor use, and beta-blocker use.
A total of 5010 patients were randomized: 2511 to valsartan and 2499 to placebo; mean follow-up was 23 months (range 0-38).

canonical_statement: The apparent adverse interaction with concomitant ACE-inhibitor and beta-blocker therapy arose from a post hoc subgroup analysis and could represent chance.

Background neurohormonal-inhibitor therapy was not controlled and randomization was stratified by beta-blocker use but not ACE-inhibitor use, so the background-therapy subgroup analysis requires caution.
Only 5% of participants were receiving spironolactone, so the trial could not assess the efficacy or safety of valsartan combined with spironolactone.
Quality of life was assessed in 60% of patients, limited to participants in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and Italy.

The authors concluded that adding valsartan to prescribed heart-failure therapy reduced the combined mortality-morbidity end point and improved clinical signs and symptoms, without reducing overall mortality.
The authors cautioned that the post hoc adverse signal in patients receiving valsartan together with an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker raised a potential safety concern that required confirmation.
The authors proposed that the approximately 5 mm Hg greater systolic blood-pressure reduction with valsartan might account for part of the observed morbidity benefit.
The trial was supported by a grant from Novartis Pharma, Basel, Switzerland.
Drs. Cohn and Tognoni reported research support and consultation arrangements with Novartis Pharmaceuticals, the study sponsor.
